title: Unit 4: Contextual Applications of Differentiation

topics.name: Rates of change in context and motion
covers: Identifying relevant mathematical information in verbal representations of real-world problems involving rates of change
Applying understandings of differentiation to problems involving motion
Generalizing understandings of motion problems to other situations involving rates of change

guide.title: Contextual applications of differentiation: review guide
guide.intro: Derivatives describe real rates: speed, growth, flow. This unit interprets them in context, links rates that change together, and uses tangent lines and L'Hospital's rule.

sections.title: Rates in context and motion
body: A derivative's units are output units per input unit. If V(t) is liters and t is minutes, V′(t) is liters per minute. Describe it as how fast the quantity is changing at that instant.
points: Position s(t), velocity v(t) = s′(t), acceleration a(t) = v′(t).
Speeding up when v and a have the same sign. Slowing down when they have opposite signs.

sections.title: Related rates
body: Write an equation relating the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to t, then substitute the known values. Substitute only after differentiating.
points: List the given rates and the wanted rate with units.
Use the Pythagorean theorem, area, or volume formulas to link variables.

sections.title: Local linearity and L'Hospital's rule
body: Near x = a, a differentiable function is close to its tangent line, so f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a).
If a limit has the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, L'Hospital's rule lets you replace f/g with f′/g′. Differentiate the top and bottom separately (not with the quotient rule).
points: Check the form before every application of L'Hospital's rule.

example.prompt: A balloon's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast is its volume growing when r = 4 cm?
example.solution: V = (4/3)πr³, so dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt = 4π(16)(0.5) = 32π cm³/s ≈ 100.5 cm³/s.

misconceptions: Slowing down depends on whether velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
Substituting first turns changing quantities into constants, whose rates are 0.
Differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is s(t) = t² − 6t meters at time t seconds. What is its velocity at t = 2?
questions.explanation: v(t) = s′(t) = 2t − 6, so v(2) = −2 m/s. The negative sign means it is moving in the negative direction.
choiceExplanations: 2 m/s is the speed. Velocity keeps the sign, which shows direction.
−4 m/s is the average velocity from t = 0 to t = 2. The question asks for the velocity at the instant t = 2.
−8 m is the position s(2), not the velocity.

questions.prompt: V(t) is the volume of water in a tank, in liters, t minutes after noon. What does V′(5) = −3 mean?
choices: At 5 minutes after noon, the tank holds 3 liters less than it did at noon
The volume decreases by 3 liters every minute after noon
At 5 minutes after noon, the volume is decreasing at 3 liters per minute
At 5 minutes after noon, the tank holds −3 liters
questions.explanation: V′(5) is the instantaneous rate of change of volume at t = 5, in liters per minute. Negative means the volume is going down at that moment.
choiceExplanations: A total change since noon would come from V(5) − V(0), not from V′(5).
V′(5) describes only the instant t = 5. The rate may be different at other times.
V′ is a rate, not an amount, and a volume cannot be negative.

questions.prompt: Use the tangent line to f(x) = √x at x = 4 to approximate √4.2.
choiceExplanations: This adds the slope 1/4 instead of the slope times the change in x.
This keeps only f(4) and leaves out the correction term f′(4)(x − 4).
This adds the change in x (0.2) directly, as if the slope were 1.

questions.prompt: A circle's radius is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is its area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?
questions.explanation: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s.
choiceExplanations: 4π leaves out r: it uses 2π · dr/dt.
25π is the area when r = 5, not its rate of change.
10π leaves out dr/dt: it uses 2πr.

questions.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0, so use L'Hospital's rule: lim x→0 2e^(2x)/1 = 2.
choiceExplanations: 1 forgets the chain rule factor of 2 when differentiating e^(2x).
0/0 is not 0. It is an indeterminate form that needs more work.
0/0 does not mean the limit fails to exist. L'Hospital's rule gives 2.

questions.prompt: A particle's velocity is v(t) = t² − 4t + 3. At t = 2.5, is it speeding up or slowing down?
choices: Slowing down, because v and a have opposite signs
questions.explanation: v(2.5) = 6.25 − 10 + 3 = −0.75 and a(t) = 2t − 4, so a(2.5) = 1. The signs are opposite, so the speed is decreasing.
choiceExplanations: The sign of v alone does not decide it either.
The sign of a alone does not decide it. Compare the signs of v and a.
v(2.5) = −0.75, which is not 0, so the particle is moving.

questions.prompt: A 10 ft ladder leans against a wall. Its bottom slides away from the wall at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down the wall when the bottom is 6 ft from the wall?
questions.explanation: x² + y² = 100. When x = 6, y = 8. Differentiating: 2x · dx/dt + 2y · dy/dt = 0, so dy/dt = −(6)(2)/8 = −1.5. The top slides down at 1.5 ft/s.
choiceExplanations: The top and bottom do not move at the same rate. Their rates are linked through x² + y² = 100.
8/3 inverts the ratio (y/x instead of x/y).
0.75 is x/y = 6/8 without multiplying by dx/dt = 2.

questions.prompt: What is lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x²?
questions.explanation: The form is 0/0. L'Hospital's rule gives sin x/(2x), still 0/0. Apply it again: cos x/2 → 1/2.
choiceExplanations: 1 forgets the factor of 2 from differentiating x².
After one application the form is still 0/0, which is not the same as 0. Apply the rule again.
Repeated 0/0 forms are handled by applying the rule again. The limit exists and equals 1/2.
